'''Wilbur Joe''' "'''Kansas Joe'''" '''McCoy'''<ref name="bare">{{cite book| first1= Bob| last1= Eagle| first2= Eric S.| last2= LeBlanc| year= 2013| title= Blues: A Regional Experience| publisher= Praeger | location= Santa Barbara, California| pages=218 | isbn= 978-0313344237}}</ref> (May 11, 1905 – January 28, 1950)<ref name="amg">{{cite web|author=Ankeny, Jason |url=http://www.allmusic.com/artist/kansas-joe-mccoy-mn0000172734/biography |title=Kansas Joe McCoy: Biography |publisher=[[AllMusic]] |access-date=2015-08-30}}</ref> was an American [[Delta blues]] singer, musician and songwriter.<ref name="Music">{{cite book
| first= Paul
| last= Du Noyer
| year= 2003
| title= The Illustrated Encyclopedia of Music
| publisher= Flame Tree Publishing 
| location= Fulham, London
| isbn= 1-904041-96-5
| page= 181}}</ref>

==Career==
McCoy performed under various stage names but is best known as Kansas Joe McCoy.<ref name="LarkinBlues">{{cite book|title=[[Encyclopedia of Popular Music|The Guinness Who's Who of Blues]]|editor=[[Colin Larkin (writer)|Colin Larkin]]|publisher=[[Guinness Publishing]]|date=1995|edition=Second|isbn=0-85112-673-1|page=260}}</ref> Born in [[Raymond, Mississippi]],<ref name="LarkinBlues"/> he was the older brother of the blues accompanist [[Papa Charlie McCoy]]. As a young man, McCoy was drawn to the music scene in [[Memphis, Tennessee]], where he played guitar and sang during the 1920s. He teamed up his with future wife, Lizzie Douglas, a guitarist better known as [[Memphis Minnie]],<ref name="LarkinBlues"/> and their 1930 recording of the song "Bumble Bee" for [[Columbia Records]] was a [[hit record|hit]].<ref>Garon, Paul (1992). ''Woman with Guitar: Memphis Minnie's Blues''. Da Capo Press. p. 25. {{ISBN|0-306-80460-3}}.</ref><ref name="Russell 2">{{cite book|first=Tony|last=Russell|year=1997|title=The Blues: From Robert Johnson to Robert Cray|publisher=Carlton Books |location=Dubai|page=12|isbn=1-85868-255-X}}</ref> In 1930, the couple moved to Chicago, where they were an important part of the burgeoning blues scene there.<ref name="LarkinBlues"/> After they were divorced, McCoy teamed up with his brother to form the [[Harlem Hamfats]], a band that performed and recorded during the second half of the 1930s.<ref name="LarkinBlues"/>

In 1936, the Harlem Hamfats released their recording of the song "The Weed Smoker's Dream". McCoy later refined the tune, changed the lyrics and retitled the song "[[Why Don't You Do Right?]]" for [[Lil Green]], who recorded it in 1941. It was [[cover version|covered]] a year later by both [[Benny Goodman]] and [[Peggy Lee]], becoming Lee's first [[hit single]]. "Why Don't You Do Right?" remains a [[jazz standard]] and is McCoy's most enduring composition.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.allmusic.com/search/all/Why+Don%27t+You+Do+Right|title=Search for "Why Don't You Do Right"|website=[[AllMusic]]|access-date=March 8, 2021}}</ref>

At the outbreak of [[World War II]] Charlie McCoy entered the military, but a heart condition kept Joe McCoy from service. He formed a band, Big Joe and his Rhythm, which performed during most of the 1940s. The band featured [[Robert Lee McCollum|Robert Nighthawk]] on harmonica and Charlie McCoy on [[mandolin]].<ref name="russell"/>

==Death and legacy==
[[File:Grave of Kansas Joe McCoy (1905–1950) at Restvale Cemetery, Alsip, IL.jpg|thumb|right|200px|McCoy's grave at Restvale Cemetery]]

McCoy died of [[heart disease]] in Chicago in 1950, at the age of 44, only a few months before Charlie died. They are both buried in [[Burr Oak Cemetery and Restvale Cemetery|Restvale Cemetery]], in [[Alsip, Illinois]].

[[Led Zeppelin]] vocalist [[Robert Plant]] took a recording of "[[When the Levee Breaks]]", by McCoy and Memphis Minnie, which was in his personal collection, to guitarist [[Jimmy Page]], who revamped the music, and the band recorded it, with most of the original lyrics, for Led Zeppelin's 1971 album, ''[[Led Zeppelin IV]]''. Neither writer was credited on the original album but Minnie was given credit on later pressings. 

McCoy's songs have also been covered by [[Skip James]], [[Bob Dylan]], [[John Mellencamp]], the [[The Ink Spots|Ink Spots]], [[Ella Fitzgerald]], [[Jo Ann Kelly]], [[Cleo Laine]] and [[A Perfect Circle]].

==Pseudonyms==
McCoy also performed and recorded under the names Bill Wither, Georgia Pine Boy, Hallelujah Joe, Big Joe McCoy and His Washboard Band, and the Mississippi Mudder.<ref name="russell">{{cite book
| first= Tony
| last= Russell
| year= 1997
| title= The Blues: From Robert Johnson to Robert Cray
| publisher= Carlton Books 
| location= Dubai
| pages= 140–41
| isbn= 1-85868-255-X}}</ref> He also used the names Hamfoot Ham, Hillbilly Plowboy, and Mud Dauber Joe.<ref name="amg"/>

==Posthumous recognition==
Like many blues musicians of his era, Joe McCoy's grave site was originally unmarked. A tribute concert<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.mccoybrotherstribute.com |title=McCoy Brothers Tribute |publisher=McCoyBrothersTribute.com |access-date=2015-08-30}}</ref> was held in October 2010 to celebrate the music of Joe and Charlie McCoy and to buy gravestones for each of them; they were installed on May 31, 2011.
